articles.title: Ranking the Top 30 NBA Shooters Ahead of 2026-27
articles.summary: Debating top-10-star status has become a rite of passage for NBA fandom.
articles.body:
Debating top-10-star status has become a rite of passage for NBA fandom.

But why stop there? Heading into the 2026-27 season, the B/R NBA staff is ready to litigate who's who among the Association's best—not only from an all-around perspective but also in several skill categories.

For this exercise, we asked voters to rank players, weighting three-point shooting at roughly 65 percent and mid-range shooting at 35 percent.

As in seasons past, we're not predicting where players will finish in April. This is a breakdown of where the league stands right now, meaning players set to start the year sidelined or unsigned aren't included. Sorry, Seth Curry.

Also check out: Ranking the 99 Best NBA Players (including our methodology) Ranking the Top 30 NBA Shooters

30. Trey Murphy III, New Orleans Pelicans

Career Stats: 45.9 FG%, 38.2 3P%, 57.2 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 47.0 FG%, 37.9 3P%, 57.2 eFG%

No, dunks don't count toward a player's shooting ability for our purposes. If they did, Trey Murphy III would be at least a dozen spots higher. Out of all the flamethrowers on this list, he's the one most likely to pass up a triple in order to posterize a hapless opponent.

Despite spending most of his career with an underwhelming set of New Orleans Pelicans teammates, Murphy has settled in as one of the more consistent long-range threats around. He topped out at 40.6 percent from deep in 2022-23 and has gradually lost some of his efficiency as his role has grown and his shot quality has decreased.

Get him onto a team with real setup men and a more functional system, and Murphy could easily rack up 25.0 points per game while threatening a 50/40/90 shooting split.

Career Stats: 45.3 FG%, 39.5 3P%, 53.0 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 45.5 FG%, 37.5 3P%, 53.8 eFG%

Willowy 6'3" guards with limited athleticism can't average at least 20.0 points per game for 10 straight seasons unless they're deadly from the perimeter.

Last year, CJ McCollum's 20-point streak came to an end as he averaged 18.7 points for the Wizards and Hawks, but that had more to do with a dip in minutes than a decline in skill. McCollum still shot 45.5 percent from the field on a steady diet of jumpers, and the champion Knicks know how dangerous he is in the clutch .

McCollum has always had enough shake to create pull-up chances, and he shot 37.6 percent on off-the-dribble treys last year. Rounding out his shooting profile, the 13-year vet has also consistently been one of the very best mid-range marksmen in the game.

Career Stats: 47.6 FG%, 37.7 3P%, 56.3 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.4 FG%, 38.6 3P%, 58.1 eFG%

The defense and a timely tip-in come to mind first when thinking of OG Anunoby, but the lockdown forward has also been a consistently excellent bomber since he entered the league with a 37.1 percent accuracy mark in 2017-18.

When Anunoby started to add real volume in 2020-21, bumping his deep attempts per 100 possessions from 5.2 to 8.8, he cemented himself as one of the top three-and-D weapons in the league. That's a label he's held ever since.

Since becoming a full-time starter in 2019-20, Anunoby has never been better than 39.8 percent or worse than 36.3 percent from long distance. Consistency like that isn't so easy to come by when you also spend most of your time wrangling the opponent's most dangerous scoring threat.

Career Stats: 46.3 FG%, 35.2 3P%, 52.0 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 45.6 FG%, 33.0 3P%, 50.7 eFG%

Devin Booker loves the mid-range, and the mid-range loves him back. While that mutual affinity won't lead to the kinds of overall efficiency numbers many of the players on this list can claim, it doesn't change the fact that the Phoenix Suns guard is lights-out inside the arc.

Over the last seven years, Booker has ranked no lower than the 91st percentile in mid-range attempt frequency for his position. In four separate seasons, he's attempted at least half of his shots from that area of the floor. Over that same seven-year span, he's made at least half of his mid-range shots four times. His worst mid-range accuracy mark since 2018-19 was 46.0 percent, still good for the 88th percentile among wings.

Analytically, these aren't great shots for most players. They work for Booker, though, and he deserves credit for knocking down the kinds of difficult self-created pull-ups most others have abandoned.

Career Stats: 47.9 FG%, 39.3 3P%, 53.8 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.8 FG%, 45.6 3P%, 57.8 eFG%

Nobody was paying attention to the Milwaukee Bucks last year—at least not to what they were doing on the court—which is probably why it'll shock many of you to learn that Bobby Portis drained damn near 46.0 percent of his threes in 2025-26.

That hit rate wasn't even a career peak. Portis knocked down 47.1 percent of his long-range tries back in 2020-21.

It's hard to decide which stat is more impressive from Portis' overlooked campaign last year—his 44.0 percent clip from above the break , or his 47.6 percent mark on pull-up threes .

Portis isn't much of a defender, and he's not going to do a whole lot of passing. But you're making a mistake if you exclude him from the conversation about the league's most reliable jump-shooters.

Career Stats: 44.9 FG%, 34.0 3P%, 50.1 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 46.1 FG%, 34.2 3P%, 51.3 eFG%

Two factors help Cade Cunningham make this list in spite of basic shooting percentages that say he doesn't belong.

The first is that the Detroit Pistons' MVP candidate has virtually no playmaking help alongside him and has to create his own looks against defenses designed specifically to make him take tough shots.

For his career, Cunningham has only been assisted on 24.9 percent of his twos and 61.3 percent of his threes. When you have to work so hard to generate scoring opportunities, efficiency is going to suffer. That he's managed the modest figures above in those circumstances speaks to his remarkable self-sufficiency.

The second factor: We know Cunningham's stroke is legit. He's at 84.0 percent from the foul line for his career and drained 39.0 percent of his treys when he fired without dribbling in 2024-25.

Career Stats: 48.3 FG%, 36.8 3P%, 56.9 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 49.0 FG%, 36.0 3P%, 56.7 eFG%

Austin Reaves earned his four-year, $180 million extension in July largely because he proved last season he could run an offense as a first option. No one should forget that the undrafted guard originally carved out a niche with the Lakers by shooting 39.8 percent from deep way back in his second season.

Last year's 46.2 percent hit rate on wide-open threes suggests Reaves hasn't lost any of his reliability at a standstill. It's just that he's advanced to the point where he rarely gets those clean looks anymore.

A healthy Luka Dončić could help Reaves tap back into his skills as a spot-up threat.

Career Stats: 45.7 FG%, 39.6 3P%, 57.5 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.0 FG%, 43.0 3P%, 59.6 eFG%

Despite a slow start in his first year with the Nuggets, Cam Johnson wound up producing one of the best shooting seasons in the league last year.

Among those with enough attempts to qualify for the three-point percentage leaderboard in 2025-26, Johnson was one of just five players to average at least 2.0 made threes per game while shooting over 43.0 percent. His 53.9 two-point field-goal percentage was the highest within that quintet.

Life for dependent scorers is very good alongside Nikola Jokić and his unmatched ability to deliver the ball directly to the shooting pocket. Johnson posted an elite 63.9 effective field-goal percentage on spot-ups last season.

Career Stats: 45.8 FG%, 37.0 3P%, 54.7 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 47.7 FG%, 35.5 3P%, 54.8 eFG%

Karl-Anthony Towns had better not get comfortable being regarded as the best big-man shooter in the game. If Lauri Markkanen finally starts piling up some volume on a Utah Jazz team that is actually trying to win, he has a great chance to steal that moniker.

Quietly, Markkanen enters this season with 27 more career threes than KAT in 228 fewer games.

Because Markkanen is so much more versatile as a shooter—uniquely capable at his size of running off screens and working in handoff actions—he should continue to outpace Towns in the volume department. Unlike KAT, who mostly depends on spot-ups and pick-and-pops, Markkanen has the mobility that allows him to be featured as a long-range weapon in a variety of ways.

If the more competitive environment in Utah brings out the best of Markkanen, turning him into the guy with three seasons of at least 39.1 percent shooting from deep rather than the guy who hovered around 35.0 percent the last two years, this ranking will be way too low.

Career Stats: 52.2 FG%, 39.7 3P%, 57.5 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 50.1 FG%, 36.8 3P%, 55.6 eFG%

Karl-Anthony Towns has more seasons shooting at least 40.0 percent from beyond the arc than any other 7-footer (minimum 35 games played per season), which goes a long way toward solidifying him as the best big-man shooter of all time.

Detractors might point to KAT's relatively low volume from deep, but he's still a pretty good bet to beat Dirk Nowitzki's current record of 1,982 triples for a 7-footer. Towns is about two-thirds of the way there and has played fewer than half of Nowitzki's career 1,522 games.

Prior to stretching his game out beyond the arc, Towns was an elite mid-range shooter. In his first four seasons, he hit between 45.0 and 48.0 percent of his two-point jumpers. As five-out spacing became more of a cheat code, KAT mostly exchanged those looks for threes and driving layups.

It's still nice to know he can do damage around the elbows if he needs to.

Career Stats: 49.3 FG%, 39.8 3P%, 59.1 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 46.3 FG%, 36.3 3P%, 55.5 eFG%

Michael Porter Jr. isn't any worse of a shooter today than he was during his first few seasons, but he's a good case study for what happens when a player has to go from specialist to top option.

In his early days with the Denver Nuggets, MPJ had the good fortune of playing with Nikola Jokić. It's no wonder he became an elite catch-and-shoot weapon, hitting at least 39.5 percent of his threes in every healthy season with the Nuggets. He peaked at a ridiculous 44.5 percent in 2020-21.

Upon joining the Brooklyn Nets, Porter had to do a lot more self-creation. He excelled, averaging 24.2 points per game, but saw his efficiency slip in the process.

Perhaps the best indicator of MPJ's incredible shooting talent: No one attempted more tightly contested threes in 2025-26, and Porter hit those shots at an absurd 41.2 percent clip.

Career Stats: 47.5 FG%, 40.7 3P%, 56.3 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.4 FG%, 39.1 3P%, 55.3 eFG%

Desmond Bane's career got off to a historic shooting start. Only he and Duncan Robinson have ever hit over 500 threes in their first three seasons at a clip of at least 42.0 percent.

It's not as if Bane dropped off after such a strong beginning, either. He's been good for at least a 38.1 percent knockdown rate in each of the last three years and has figured out ways to compensate for his short wingspan. Few shots fall as reliably as Bane's side-step three-pointer.

Because he's such a dangerous catch-and-shoot threat, opponents recklessly sprint at Bane if he receives a pass in space. Rather than take on a rangy wing by trying to shoot over the top, Bane has perfected the art of faking, calmly moving laterally and drilling the open look his patience created.

Career Stats: 49.9 FG%, 39.1 3P%, 55.6 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 50.5 FG%, 38.7 3P%, 57.3 eFG%

Just imagine how much higher Kawhi Leonard would rank if somebody had introduced him to the three-point shot a little earlier in his career.

Last season was the first time Leonard had ever attempted at least 7.0 threes per 36 minutes, and the high-volume style from long range agreed with him. At 34, he set a new personal best in true shooting percentage and reached a new career high at 27.9 points per game.

Leonard's jumper lasers into the basket, defying every coach who ever preached to shooters about a high-arcing ball flight. You wouldn't teach anyone to fire away with the trajectory Leonard prefers, but the results are impossible to deny.

Kevin Durant and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were the only players with higher field-goal percentages on pull-up shots (minimum 600 attempts) last season.

Career Stats: 47.7 FG%, 39.2 3P%, 57.4 eFG%

2024-25 Stats: 47.3 FG%, 38.8 3P%, 58.2 eFG%

Increased volume during his breakout with the Indiana Pacers knocked Tyrese Haliburton's long-range accuracy mark below 40.0 percent for the first time in 2023-24. Nobody is complaining, as Hali's increased willingness to fire off the dribble was integral to the offensive explosion that ultimately got Indy to the 2025 Finals.

An absolute craftsman as a passer, Haliburton doesn't get enough credit for the breadth of jumpers he's able to create inside the arc. During his last two healthy seasons with the Pacers, Haliburton rated in the 98th percentile on mid-rangers for his position.

Fans of most opposing teams will tell you that figure feels low. In the biggest moments, Hali's step-back jumper going right seems to fall 100 percent of the time.

Career Stats: 45.4 FG%, 38.9 3P%, 53.2 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 46.0 FG%, 39.6 3P%, 55.1 eFG%

Throw out his rookie season, which featured a relatively solid 35.5 percent mark from three, and Darius Garland has been good for at least 37.1 percent from deep on good volume in every year of his career.

If last season's post-deadline cameo with the LA Clippers is any indication, he's only just now approaching his peak as a shooter. In 19 games with his new team, Garland nailed 43.8 percent of his treys on what would have been a career-high 7.6 attempts per game.

Though you might think Garland's lack of size would make it tougher for him to hit jumpers inside the arc, he's been a reliable scorer on mid-rangers and has been especially accurate on those tricky short pull-ups and runners. In each of the last two seasons, he's hit over 50.0 percent of his short mid-rangers.

Career Stats: 46.1 FG%, 37.7 3P%, 53.4 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 46.2 FG%, 36.7 3P%, 53.6 eFG%

Tyrese Maxey's role over the last couple of years has knocked his efficiency down, perhaps to the point that some will take issue with his inclusion here. Just keep in mind that he shot 42.7 percent and 43.4 percent from deep in 2021-22 and 2022-23, respectively, which was the last time he wasn't tasked with playing ridiculous minutes and running the show for Philadelphia.

Back in those days, roughly 70.0 percent of Maxey's threes came via assists. That number has been closer to 55.0 percent over the last two seasons. This year's Sixers have a broader array of threats and should help get Maxey back to his best self from the perimeter.

If we were rating shooters strictly on the strength of what they can do when going downhill at full speed, Maxey would certainly climb the rankings. Nobody is better at softly dropping floaters at a dead run, often from as far out as 10-15 feet.

Career Stats: 43.7 FG%, 39.9 3P%, 59.7 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 45.6 FG%, 41.0 3P%, 61.3 eFG%

Duncan Robinson's 2019-20 season was a revelation, as the undrafted 25-year-old established himself as one of the league's preeminent movement shooters.

He canned 44.6 percent of his treys for the Miami Heat that year, many of which were about as difficult as catch-and-shoot attempts get. Robinson isn't much of a self-starter with the ball, but his ability to sprint around screens, rise and fire sets him apart from all but a handful of gunners around the NBA.

If anything, his 39.9 percent career mark from beyond the stripe undersells Robinson's true shooting ability. The types of triples he has subsisted on are just harder than your run-of-the-mill corner looks many other specialists settle for.

As an added bonus, Robinson is particularly adept at the above-the-break threes many defenses are more willing to concede. He hit 42.0 percent of those looks last season, good for the 94th percentile among wings.

13. Donovan Mitchell, Cleveland Cavaliers

Career Stats: 45.3 FG%, 36.6 3P%, 53.0 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.3 FG%, 36.4 3P%, 56.3 eFG%

Donovan Mitchell and Stephen Curry are the only players to average at least 3.0 made three-pointers per game in each of the last six seasons. While Mitchell doesn't come close to Curry in terms of accuracy, his volume of attempts on slightly better than league-average percentages is more than enough to command maximum defensive attention.

In addition to his deep shooting, Mitchell has developed into a much more dangerous mid-range shot-maker during the last few seasons. In 2025-26, his 52.0 percent conversion rate on all mid-range jumpers ranked in the 95th percentile among combo guards.

If aesthetics count for anything here, they certainly help Mitchell's case. He has always had remarkably smooth lift on his jumpers and shoots what close observers of shot mechanics would call an "easy ball." With great power from his lower half, Mitchell can fire it from extremely deep, seemingly without any effort at all.

Career Stats: 47.4 FG%, 39.4 3P%, 54.0 eFG%

2024-25 Stats: 47.3 FG%, 40.1 3P%, 54.9 eFG%

It'd be nice if we could compliment Kyrie Irving for his shooting consistency over a 14-year career, but it's not technically accurate to say he's sustained his accuracy from all over the floor.

Believe it or not, Irving's effective field-goal percentage was higher during his two years in Boston than it was in his first six seasons with the Cavs. It climbed again during Irving's four-year tour with Brooklyn before ticking up another few points in 128 games (so far) in Dallas.

Incredible ball-handling frees up Irving to get to two-point jumpers and floaters whenever he wants, and opponents have no choice but to stay close to him because of his consistent ability to drain 40.0 percent of his threes.

Though it's not a major component of this list, Irving should get a few bonus points for the sheer variety of ways he's able to shoot the ball. Nobody else on this list has won a game on a 15-foot running hook with his off hand.

Career Stats: 46.9 FG%, 35.2 3P%, 54.4 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 47.6 FG%, 36.6 3P%, 56.3 eFG%

Luka Dončić won't win many empty-gym shooting contests, but his step-back three is among the most respected in the league. By leveraging the threat of that shot to pull defenders out into space, Dončić gets access to scoring chances everywhere on the floor.

Last season, Dončić's 7.5 pull-up three-point attempts per game led the NBA , and he shot 36.3 percent on them.

When opponents sell out to stop him from getting to his pet shots from beyond the arc, Dončić feasts in the lane. He's rated above the 86th percentile at his position on short mid-range accuracy in each of the last six seasons. Quietly, he's also deadly on long mid-rangers, where he's generally been good for about a 50.0 percent hit rate.

With an incredibly strong base, an ability to lean back and defend his release with an outstretched right leg, and no shortage of confidence, Dončić can knock down jumpers most players can't even create in the first place.

10. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Oklahoma City Thunder

Career Stats: 50.8 FG%, 36.0 3P%, 54.8 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 55.3 FG%, 38.6 3P%, 59.7 eFG%

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander isn't the kind of standstill marksman you might expect on a list like this, but he's proof that great shooters can take many forms. Among the two-time MVP's most impressive talents: his unmatched ability to generate and make jumpers in isolation.

SGA posted a 59.6 effective field-goal percentage on shots attempted after taking at least seven dribbles in 2025-26, the most efficient rate of anyone who tried at least 200 such shots. Many of those were the tough, fading twos you picture when thinking of Gilgeous-Alexander, but the two-time MVP also made a scorching 44.6 percent of the 101 threes he took after dribbling at least seven times.

Among point guards, SGA has rated in at least the 93rd percentile in mid-range accuracy for three straight years. Almost nobody is better on short bankers and step-throughs, and it feels unfair that he's also posted three-point hit rates in the high 30s across each of the last two years.

Career Stats: 46.6 FG%, 44.2 3P%, 59.5 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 53.3 FG%, 47.8 3P%, 66.5 eFG%

The rankings catch Luke Kennard at a good time, fresh off a season in which he shot a league-leading 47.8 percent from deep while splitting time between the Los Angeles Lakers and Atlanta Hawks.

Leaving Kennard uncovered is a cardinal sin for a defense. On the rare occasions he was given at least 10 feet of space in 2025-26, he drilled a ridiculous 51.9 percent of his three-point tries. That was the highest hit rate among all players who attempted as many as Kennard's 131 "wide open" threes.

Don't mistake the focus on last season as a dismissal of Kennard's much larger body of work. His worst mark for a full season is 39.4 percent, he's led the league in accuracy three times and he's been at 44.0 percent or better in five separate seasons.

Career Stats: 45.9 FG%, 39.0 3P%, 53.5 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.3 FG%, 43.5 3P%, 57.3 eFG%

Only nine active players own career three-point accuracy marks of at least 39.0 percent on over 3,500 attempts, and Jamal Murray is one of them. If you filter out the specialists who've mostly subsisted on spoon-fed setups (Duncan Robinson, Buddy Hield, Klay Thompson), the field shrinks to a point where Murray appears to be one of the half-dozen best three-point gunners of his generation.

Obviously, we need to account for the fact that Murray has spent his entire career benefittng from Nikola Jokić's assists. But Murray generates a ton of pull-up mid-rangers as a pick-and-roll ball-handler.

Over 60.0 percent of the two-point makes in his career have come without the benefit of a teammate assist, which shows just how much he's still creating on his own.

Entering his 10th season, Murray also isn't slowing down. He made his first All-Star and All-NBA teams last year while setting new career highs in three-pointers made (245) and true shooting percentage (62.2 percent).

Career Stats: 56.1 FG%, 36.2 3P%, 59.8 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 56.9 FG%, 38.0 3P%, 61.8 eFG%

This is a pretty good outcome for a player who would probably prefer not to shoot the ball at all.

Nikola Jokić's singular, generational skill as a passer defines his career and will always be the ability for which he's remembered. That makes it easy to forget that he's among the most creative and effective shooters of the basketball anyone's ever seen.

Few bigs have ever had softer touch in the short mid-range area than Jokić, whose feathery release makes him dangerous everywhere inside the arc. For some context, he's shooting 58.4 percent from 3-10 feet, 51.3 percent from 10-16 feet and 46.7 percent from 16 feet out to the three-point line for his career.

Kevin Durant is at 48.3 percent, 48.6 percent and 46.0 percent for his career, respectively .

That the 7-footer's three-point accuracy rates as an afterthought speaks to just how dangerous Jokić's shooting ability all over the floor truly is.

6. Anthony Edwards, Minnesota Timberwolves

Career Stats: 45.3 FG%, 36.9 3P%, 53.1 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 48.9 FG%, 39.9 3P%, 57.2 eFG%

Only two players—Buddy Hield and Klay Thompson—have made more total threes in the first six years of their careers than Anthony Edwards, whose degree of difficulty tends to be higher than that of his mostly catch-and-shoot peers.

The volume is doing a lot of work for Edwards' case here, as he's only at 36.9 percent from deep for his career and didn't establish himself as a better-than-average mid-range marksman until last season, when he knocked down 45.0 percent of those looks.

It shouldn't come as a surprise that Edwards added in-between accuracy to his game; year-over-year improvement has defined his career. So if his overall efficiency marks seem underwhelming, and if the volume doesn't persuade you he belongs quite this high, understand that the current version of Edwards is better than every previous one and unquestionably one of the top pure shooters in the sport.

Case in point: Last season, he was one of just three players to shoot at least 39.0 percent from deep while averaging more than 8.0 long-range attempts per game.

5. Damian Lillard, Portland Trail Blazers

Career Stats: 43.9 FG%, 37.1 3P%, 52.3 eFG%

2024-25 Stats: 44.8 FG%, 37.6 3P%, 54.7 eFG%

Fifth on the all-time list in made threes, Damian Lillard has long been regarded as the closest thing to Steph Curry in one critical sense: He's the only guy in the league who is remotely as dangerous off the dribble from the moment he crosses the half-court line.

Lillard's pull-up prowess extends defenses and has also consistently produced odds-defying game-winners on the biggest stages.

Though he doesn't do a fraction of the off-ball work Curry does, Lillard is still exceptionally challenging to defend.

Lest there be any concern about his stroke deteriorating as a result of a torn Achilles, Lillard showed up to the 2026 All-Star Game after not playing for months and won the Three-Point Contest. That honor, collected during a season in which he didn't suit up for a single game, tied him with Larry Bird and Craig Hodges as the only three-time winners in the event's history.

Career Stats: 48.5 FG%, 38.5 3P%, 54.5 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 46.7 FG%, 36.9 3P%, 53.3 eFG%

Jalen Brunson is the best illustration of how great shooting is about so much more than a flick of the wrist.

The reigning Finals MVP lands here not just because the ball always comes off his fingertips with just the right amount of spin and touch, but also because he utilizes his full body to generate looks.

Brunson's lack of size forced him to become a master of footwork, balance, timing and creativity. He uses all of it to fake, pivot and nudge his way into good angles from everywhere on the floor. Though he doesn't get to the rim much and consistently ranks well below the positional average in three-point attempt frequency , Brunson makes up for it by dominating the entire mid-range area.

Due largely to his skill at keeping defenders off balance, Brunson is also an excellent foul-drawer. That has helped him keep his true shooting percentage above the league average in each of the last six years, which probably gives a better sense of his skill level than his underwhelming effective field-goal percentage, which doesn't count free throws.

Career Stats: 47.5 FG%, 42.5 3P%, 60.1 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 47.5 FG%, 42.5 3P%, 60.1 eFG%

It wasn't quite enough to win him Rookie of the Year over former Duke teammate Cooper Flagg, but Kon Knueppel can still lay claim to the greatest shooting season ever produced by a first-year player.

In 81 games last season, Knueppel canned 273 treys, obliterating Keegan Murray's previous record of 203. At 42.5 percent, Knueppel was also more accurate than every previous rookie with at least 150 makes... other than Curry , who shot 43.7 percent en route to 166 makes back in 2009-10.

At 51.0 percent from the corners, Knueppel proved to be particularly dangerous on the catch. LaMelo Ball's exit could cut down the share of shots Knueppel takes via teammate assist, but offseason work on off-the-dribble shooting could allow for a second season just as good as his first.

Knueppel has a long way to go in terms of his all-time ranking among NBA shooters, but nobody has ever gotten off to a better start.

Career Stats: 50.3 FG%, 39.2 3P%, 55.6 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 52.0 FG%, 41.3 3P%, 58.8 eFG%

Kevin Durant has hit at least 40.0 percent from long range in four of the last five seasons, an indicator that he has a legitimate superpower as a three-point shooter.

That's pretty impressive considering he doesn't even really like to fire away from deep. KD's 2.4 made triples per game last season ranked outside the top 50, and he's never once attempted more than 32.0 percent of his shots from beyond the arc.

Durant's greatest shooting prowess comes in the disfavored mid-range area, where his proficiency makes him one of very few players for whom a pull-up two is still a valuable scoring option. He's hit at least 50.0 percent of his mid-range attempts in each of the last eight seasons, which is basically unheard of at his level of volume.

Shifty shoulders, a high release and a feathery touch make KD perhaps the league's best bailout option on offense. He can generate a good perimeter look against any defender at any time.

Career Stats: 47.1 FG%, 42.2 3P%, 58.2 eFG%

2025-26 Stats: 46.8 FG%, 39.3 3P%, 58.7 eFG%

Last year was a substandard season for Stephen Curry, whose 4.4 made threes per game would have led the league by a comfortable margin had he qualified. Hopefully that helps frame the extent to which Curry, the undisputed greatest shooter of all time, continues to distance himself from all of his peers.

No one has ever drawn more attention away from the ball than Steph. Every opponent's game plan centers on denying him touches in space, which makes his volume and accuracy all the more impressive. It's not just that Curry is the all-time leader in made triples by a mile, or that he's piled up over 4,000 makes at a 42.2 percent clip. It's that he's done so while every opponent burned maximum calories trying to stop him.

It's impossible to overstate how hard Curry has to work to get his looks, and that sets him apart from many players on this list who've sustained elite efficiency numbers on a much higher share of uncontested shots.

When it comes to shooting, there's Curry, a chasm wider than the Grand Canyon, and everyone else.

articles.title: Ranking the Top 30 NBA Defenders Ahead of 2026-27
articles.summary: Debating top-10-star status has become a rite of passage for NBA fandom.
articles.body:
Debating top-10-star status has become a rite of passage for NBA fandom.

But why stop there? Heading into the 2026-27 season, the B/R NBA staff is ready to litigate who's who among the Association's best—not only from an all-around perspective, but also in several skill categories.

As in seasons past, we're not predicting where players will finish in April. This is a breakdown of where the league stands right now, meaning players set to start the year sidelined or buried in depth charts are excluded.

Also check out: Ranking the 99 Best NBA Players (including our methodology) Ranking the Top 30 NBA Shooters

30. Robert Williams III, C, Portland Trail Blazers

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-4.3 , Steals/G: 0.6, Blocks/G: 1.5

Honors: All-Defensive 2nd Team (2021-22)

Robert Williams III may be one of two players on this list not to be a full-time starter this season, speaking more so to the Portland Trail Blazers' depth at center rather than any weaknesses on Williams' end.

Injuries have limited the soon-to-be 29-year-old's time on the court throughout his career, although Williams is absolutely one of the best rim protectors in the NBA when healthy.

Of the 100 players who defended 168 shots or more at the rim last season, Williams ranked third in opponent shooting percentage (47.0), a mark even stingier than that of Victor Wembanyama.

Although he stands at just 6'9", Williams has a massive 7'6" wingspan that allows him to swat plenty of shots (3.0 per 36 minutes for his career) and deter even more. The Blazers handed Williams a new three-year, $43.5 million contract this offseason to keep him as a defensive anchor off the bench.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-9.2 , Steals/G: 1.8, Blocks/G: 0.7

Honors: All-Defensive 2nd Team (2023-24)

Jalen Suggs is the new Derrick White, a combo guard who has some offensive chops but absolutely makes his living on the defensive side of the ball.

Suggs, 25, finished No. 4 overall in steal percentage this past season (3.2 percent), and only five qualified players topped his 1.8 swipes per game. He's nimble enough to play passing lanes and strong enough to get into the body of opposing guards, making them uncomfortable while forcing turnovers.

The Orlando Magic allowed a whopping 9.2 fewer points per 100 possessions with Suggs on the floor last season, a figure that ranked in the 97th percentile via Cleaning the Glass. Few elite rim protectors can make this kind of an impact, let alone guards.

Orlando certainly has its offensive woes, although having Suggs on the court has been the foundation of an elite defense.

28. Walker Kessler, C, Los Angeles Lakers

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-6.8 , Steals/G: 1.4, Blocks/G: 1.8

The Los Angeles Lakers are betting big on Walker Kessler being their defensive anchor in the Luka Dončić era.

Big is also the best word to describe the 7'2", 245-pound center, who's one of the most intimidating figures in the NBA. The 25-year-old has averaged 3.4 blocks per 36 minutes in his career and held opponents to just 50.0 percent shooting at the rim in 2024-25, his last (mostly) healthy season.

Kessler is truly a defensive player worthy of game-planning around. Few players are backing him down given Kessler's size and strength, and he has enough mobility around the basket to make opponents think twice when they drive inside.

Health will be worth monitoring moving forward, as Kessler's total games have dropped every year since his rookie season, including just five contests last year before shoulder surgery.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-4.0 , Steals/G: 1.1, Blocks/G: 1.4

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year (2022-23), All-Defensive 1st Team x 2 (2021-22, 2022-23), All-Defensive 2nd Team (2024-25), Block Champion x 2 (2021-22, 2022-23)

Is putting a recent Defensive Player of the Year and block champion this low an insult to Jaren Jackson Jr.? Or have others just surpassed the 27-year-old in recent seasons?

Jackson is still an awesome defender when healthy. His raw block stats aren't as gaudy as yesteryear, although the 6'10" big man still makes a huge impact around the rim (52.7 opponent field goal percentage).

He's not as mobile as players like Evan Mobley or Chet Holmgren, although Jackson has the right combination of size, strength and athleticism to be a defensive threat anywhere on the floor.

His lack of defensive rebounding certainly holds Jackson back (4.8 per game last season), and knee injuries have continued to pop up. If healthy, however, Jackson can be a defensive anchor for a Utah Jazz team looking to make a playoff push this season.

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-4.8 , Steals/G: 0.9, Blocks/G: 0.4

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2024-25)

Lu Dort served as the focal point of the Oklahoma City Thunder's defensive attack for years, finishing as high as fourth place for Defensive Player of the Year just two seasons ago.

His raw defensive numbers don't do Dort's brand of defense justice. Over the years, the 6'4", 220-pound wing has often been tasked to guard the opponent's best player, no matter their size or position. This included everyone from point guards to power forwards, as all had to battle their way out of the Dorture Chamber. Few have fared very well .

Now a member of the Atlanta Hawks due to OKC's financial constraints, the 27-year-old Dort should still be one of the best and most versatile defenders in the NBA.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-5.4 , Steals/G: 1.2, Blocks/G: 0.7

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2023-24), All-Defensive 2nd Team x 5 (2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, 2025-26)

A regular member of the All-Defensive teams over the past decade, Bam Adebayo is one of the most versatile big men in the NBA with his ability to defend one-on-one, play passing lanes and protect the rim.

The 29-year-old has registered a negative defensive swing rating in all nine of his professional seasons with the Miami Heat, with the last five all ranking in the 80th percentile or above via Cleaning the Glass . Adebayo moves well for someone his size (6'9", 255 pounds) and is able to effectively guard power forwards or centers.

A lack of elite shot blocking has probably cost Adebayo a Defensive Player of the Year trophy by now, although his impact is felt in other areas on the court.

24. Jalen Williams, F, Oklahoma City Thunder

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-0.4 , Steals/G: 1.2, Blocks/G: 0.3

Honors: All-Defensive 2nd Team (2024-25)

One of the few players on this list whose offensive game is even better than his defensive one, a healthy Jalen Williams is one of the best young players in the NBA.

Defensively, Williams relies on his size (6'5", 211 pounds), wingspan (7'2") and excellent hands to thrive. He excels in one-on-one coverage, poking balls away in isolation situations that lead to steals either for himself or a teammate. His 1.6 steals per game were good for seventh overall in 2024-25.

Williams moves his feet well enough to keep opponents in front of him, interrupting potential drives and creation opportunities. He should have an even bigger defensive responsibility this season now that Lu Dort has been traded to the Atlanta Hawks.

23. Mitchell Robinson, C, Boston Celtics

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-1.0 , Steals/G: 0.9, Blocks/G: 1.2

Few players look the part of "defensive anchor" more than Mitchell Robinson.

At 7'0" and 240 pounds with a 7'4" wingspan, Robinson is a classic rim protector who thrives on contesting shots all over the court. Opponents shot a measly 50.9 percent at the rim last season with Robinson defending, as the 28-year-old also racked up 1.7 steals, 2.1 blocks and 16.1 rebounds per 36 minutes of play.

His defense was a big reason for the New York Knicks' success in the playoffs, as Robinson did an admirable job on centers like Victor Wembanyama and Joel Embiid while breaking up passing lanes and denying would-be drivers at the rim.

With Robinson now in Boston, the Knicks defense is going to take a big hit this season.

22. Jarrett Allen, C, Cleveland Cavaliers

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-0.2 , Steals/G: 1.0, Blocks/G: 0.8

Jarrett Allen has been one of the NBA's most underrated defenders for years now, often sacrificing the spotlight to teammate Evan Mobley.

There's a reason why the Cleveland Cavaliers have refused to trade Allen and move Mobley to a full-time center position, however. Allen's ability to protect the rim, play passing lanes and defend outside of the paint all help Mobley serve as a free safety and keep him from guarding the more physical centers in the league.

Allen held opponents to worse shooting from all areas of the court last season (4.3 percentage points, according to NBA.com's tracking data ), including a 9.5 point drop within six feet (down to 54.1 percent). There's essentially nothing Allen doesn't do defensively, as he's finished in the top 12 in Defensive Player of the Year voting three times in his career.

21. Isaiah Hartenstein, C, Oklahoma City Thunder

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-4.7 , Steals/G: 1.0, Blocks/G: 0.8

Isaiah Hartenstein plays a similar role to Jarrett Allen, as he provides the backbone of the defense so Chet Holmgren can focus on being a roaming defender and not have to guard more physical centers.

The Oklahoma City Thunder have a defensive rating of 104.7 with Holmgren on the court without Hartenstein (still elite!), yet this number drops to 100.7 (100th percentile via Cleaning the Glass ) when both big men share the floor.

Hartenstein is a big, strong 7-footer who can match up with nearly every center in the NBA. While not a premier shot-blocker like Holmgren, Hartenstein still held opponents to just 54.1 percent shooting at the rim and is one of the better rebounders in the NBA.

20. Anthony Davis, F/C, Washington Wizards

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-1.9 , Steals/G: 1.1, Blocks/G: 1.7

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team x 3 (2017-18, 2019-20, 2023-24), All-Defensive 2nd Team x 2 (2014-15, 2016-17), Block Champion x 3 (2013-14, 2014-15, 2017-18)

Anthony Davis is one of the most accomplished defenders on this list, finishing as high as No. 2 in Defensive Player of the Year voting and being voted in the top 10 a total of six times.

Davis is a few years removed from his prime, but can still be the anchor of a team when healthy. His 6'10", 253-pound frame and near 7'6" wingspan are built for not only protecting the rim but also racking up steals.

Davis would have ranked in the top five in blocks per game and defensive rebounds (8.0) last season had he logged enough court time to qualify, as the 33-year-old is proving he can still produce at a high level when healthy.

This year will perhaps be the greatest challenge of Davis' career, as he's now tasked with turning around a Washington Wizards defense that ranked dead last in the NBA with a 122.7 rating.

19. Draymond Green, F/C, Golden State Warriors

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-2.1 , Steals/G: 0.9, Blocks/G: 0.6

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year (2016-17), All-Defensive 1st Team x 5, (2014-15, 2015-16, 2016-17, 2020-21, 2024-25), All-Defensive 2nd Team x 4 (2017-18, 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23), Steals Champion (2016-17)

Draymond Green hit his defensive peak about a decade ago, although the 36-year-old can still cause a lot of disruption for opposing offenses.

Green's primary strength has always been his versatility. He has enough size at 6'6" and 230 pounds to challenge big men inside, yet has been mobile enough to switch everything and stay in front of quicker guards. A 7'1" wingspan has helped as well.

A third-place finisher in Defensive Player of the Year just two seasons ago, Green could break a tie with players like Hakeem Olajuwon, Rudy Gobert, Michael Jordan and others if he is named to his 10th All-Defense team this year.

18. Donovan Clingan, C, Portland Trail Blazers

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-0.2 , Steals/G: 0.6, Blocks/G: 1.7

Donovan Clingan is now the second Portland Trail Blazers center to make this list, and the combination of him and Robert Williams III will be a nightmare for opponents to drive inside against.

Clingan is a giant at 7'2" and 280 pounds, as his mere presence helps deter opponents from trying anything around the rim. The 22-year-old's 1.7 blocks per game ranked fifth-highest in the NBA while Clingan's 11.6 total rebounds per game were good for third.

The third-year pro isn't as mobile as some of the other elite rim protectors in the NBA. Still, Clingan is one of the youngest players included here, and he led the entire league in shots contested at the rim (470).

17. Jaden McDaniels, F, Minnesota Timberwolves

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-0.1 , Steals/G: 1.1, Blocks/G: 1.0

Stick Jaden McDaniels on a number of All-Star guards and wings and he'll make them look like a second-grader learning how to dribble. One of the premier defensive wings in the NBA at 6'9" and with a 7-foot wingspan, McDaniels has yet to meet a one-on-one assignment he couldn't handle.

The 26-year-old is exactly the type of defender who teams crave in the playoffs when the pace slows down and play becomes isolation-heavy. McDaniels can legitimately defend four different positions and was one of just eight players last season to average a full block and steal per game.

Adding muscle to his 185-pound frame would help McDaniels with some of the bigger wings in the NBA, although he's nimble enough now to stick to the quickest of guards.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-6.6 , Steals/G: 1.9, Blocks/G: 0.6

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year x 2 (2014-15, 2015-16), All-Defensive 1st Team x 3 (2014-15, 2015-16, 2016-17), All-Defensive 2nd Team x 4 (2013-14, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21), Steals Champion (2014-15)

Although he turned 35 this past summer, Kawhi Leonard is looking nearly as good as ever on both sides of the ball.

What Leonard has lost in quickness he's made up for in strength, as the two-time Finals MVP can still defend multiple positions with his 6'6" frame and massive 7'3" wingspan. His 1.9 steals per game ranked No. 4 overall in the NBA this past season.

Health will continue to be an issue, although Leonard is still an elite defender when he's on the floor. Last season was the fifth time in his career Leonard registered a defensive swing rating in the 90th percentile or better (93rd percentile, via Cleaning the Glass ).

Swapping out Brandon Ingram for Leonard is a huge upgrade, especially on the defensive end.

15. Toumani Camara, F, Portland Trail Blazers

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-0.4, Steals/G: 1.1, Blocks/G: 0.4

Despite being the No. 52 overall pick in 2023, Toumani Camara became a full-time starter as a rookie because of his defensive prowess. With a backcourt of Ja Morant and 36-year-old Damian Lillard coming off a torn Achilles, the Portland Trail Blazers will need Camara now more than ever.

A 6'7", 230-pound wing, Camara can defend nearly everything and everyone. He's a taller version of Lu Dort and a stronger version of Jaden McDaniels who also played all 82 games last season.

Armed with a 7'1" wingspan, Camara held opponents to just 33.5 percent shooting on three-pointers last season, a full 3.1 percentage points below their average.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-4.6 , Steals/G: 2.0, Blocks/G: 0.4

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2024-25), All-Defensive 2nd Team (2025-26), Steals Champion (2024-25)

With Trae Young gone and Dyson Daniels holding down a backcourt spot, the Atlanta Hawks went from the NBA's worst point-of-attack defender to one of its best.

Daniels is a nightmare for opposing ball-handlers, as he's a huge guard (6'7", 6'10½" wingspan) who doesn't sacrifice mobility. He has some of the best hands and instincts in all of basketball, knowing the precise moment to go for a turnover and when to play it safe and stop a driving attempt instead.

Daniels finished just short of a second straight steals title this season (1.96 per game compared to Ausar Thompson's 2.0), a year after he led the NBA with a whopping 3.0 per contest. Only seven other players in the history of the league have averaged three or more steals over the course of a season, a list that includes Michael Jordan and John Stockton.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-9.6 , Steals/G: 1.1, Blocks/G: 1.3

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2025-26), All-Defensive 2nd Team x 2 (2022-23, 2023-24)

Although he turned 32 this past summer, Derrick White only seems to be getting better defensively with age.

White not only made his first All-Defensive first team this past year but also finished sixth overall in Defensive Player of the Year voting, the highest placing among all NBA guards.

Jaylen Brown deservedly got most of the credit for keeping the Boston Celtics at the top of the East without Jayson Tatum for the majority of the season, although White's defense was a huge part as well. Boston allowed nearly 10 fewer points per 100 possessions with White on the floor, good for the 97th percentile among all players per Cleaning the Glass .

White isn't your typical one-dimensional backcourt defender, as he's one of the best shot-blocking guards in NBA history and perhaps the best we've seen since Dwyane Wade. White's 1.3 blocks per game somehow ranked 15th overall in the NBA among all positions, topping even big men like Mitchell Robinson, Jalen Duren and Brook Lopez.

12. Collin Murray-Boyles, F/C, Toronto Raptors

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-3.0, Steals/G: 0.9, Blocks/G: 0.9

Collin Murray-Boyles is going to be a huge part of a ferocious Toronto Raptors defense for years to come.

Just a rookie last season, Murray-Boyles already showed off the entire defensive toolbox, especially in his first taste of the playoffs against the Cleveland Cavaliers.

He's big enough to play both power forward and center and athletic enough to switch onto guards at the perimeter. Excellent hands accompany a near 7'1" wingspan, allowing Murray-Boyles to be one of the most versatile big-men defenders in the entire NBA already.

After coming into the league a little heavy at 245 pounds for his modest 6'7" frame, Murray-Boyles said he's lost a substantial amount of weight heading into Year 2, taking up distance running and embracing a healthier diet this offseason per TSN's Josh Lewenberg .

Still just 21, Murray-Boyles is going to become a household name very soon.

11. Alex Caruso, G, Oklahoma City Thunder

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-7.0 , Steals/G: 1.3, Blocks/G: 0.3

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2022-23), All-Defensive 2nd Team (2023-24)

For those at home counting, this is the third current member of the Oklahoma City Thunder on this list, and we're not even close to being done.

Alex Caruso's role may have dipped on a loaded Thunder squad, although his individual and team defense remains elite. A 3.4 steal percentage would have ranked No. 3 overall in the NBA had Caruso logged enough court time to qualify, and the 32-year-old led the NBA in steal percentage during both of his All-Defensive seasons with the Chicago Bulls.

A defensive swing rating in the 94th percentile last season was the fifth time in nine seasons Caruso has ranked in the 90s or above, with eight of the nine coming in the 80th percentile or better, via Cleaning the Glass .

A bulldog of a ball-stopper, Caruso still isn't a top-two defender on his own team, however.

10. Giannis Antetokounmpo, F, Miami Heat

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-5.7 , Steals/G: 0.9, Blocks/G: 0.7

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year (2019-20), All-Defensive 1st Team x 4 (2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22), All-Defensive 2nd Team (2016-17)

Giannis Antetokounmpo's incredible offensive game will naturally garner most of the attention, although the 31-year-old has also become one of the premier defenders of the past decade.

Despite his mild block numbers, the 6'11" Antetokounmpo has long been a premier rim protector, holding opponents to just 51.5 percent shooting at the basket this past season. Few players have Antetokounmpo's combination of size and strength, as his body transformation since coming into the NBA as a lanky teenager has been incredible.

After years of getting to play alongside another elite defender in Brook Lopez, Antetokounmpo gets to join forces with Bam Adebayo in the Miami Heat frontcourt. Both can ease the pressure off the other and are able to take turns going to battle with the toughest of offensive opponents.

9. Cason Wallace, G, Oklahoma City Thunder

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-3.5 , Steals/G: 1.9, Blocks/G: 0.4

Honors: All-Defensive 2nd Team (2025-26)

Placing Cason Wallace in the top 10 at just 22 years old is a testament to his defensive work already and the projected increase in role with Lu Dort traded to the Atlanta Hawks.

Wallace ranked second in steal percentage (3.5 percent) and third in steals per game (1.9) this past season despite only starting 58 of his 77 games. In those 58 starts, Wallace racked up 2.1 steals per contest, which would have led the NBA.

Wallace will likely start this season in place of Dort, sliding between Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Jalen Williams. He'll continually draw the toughest backcourt assignment, helping to keep Gilgeous-Alexander fresh for another long playoff run.

A strong, quick guard with terrific hands, Wallace has been an elite defender from the day he stepped onto an NBA court. He finally gets the chance to prove it as a full-time starter for the first time in his four-year career.

8. Evan Mobley, F/C, Cleveland Cavaliers

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-4.2 , Steals/G: 0.7, Blocks/G: 1.7

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year (2024-25), All-Defensive 1st Team (2022-23, 2024-25)

Still just 25, Evan Mobley already has a DPOY trophy and a pair of All-Defensive first-team honors to his name. He somehow got snubbed for a team this past season, despite having more blocks per game and a better defensive swing rating than in his Defensive Player of the Year season.

Mobley's best defensive strength when entering the NBA was his switchability as a 6'11" big man out of USC. Now, he can still guard all five positions and some added muscle has turned him into an elite rim protector as well.

Mobley's 1.7 blocks per game ranked No. 4 overall in the NBA while his 48.7 percent opponent shooting at the rim was the second-lowest of the top-56 total shot contesters.

A monster in every area of the defensive end, Mobley is still getting better as he looks to fill up his trophy case.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-3.9 , Steals/G: 1.6, Blocks/G: 0.7

Honors : All-Defensive 2nd Team x 2 (2022-23, 2025-26), Steals Champion (2022-23)

How do you build a strong defense around Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns? Fill in the gaps with elite wings like OG Anunoby.

The 29-year-old has been one of the premier defenders of this decade, using his 6'7" frame and 7'2" wingspan to shut down would-be drivers, play passing lanes and switch onto bigger opponents as needed.

Anunoby is excellent at playing individual and team defense, using his superb instincts to know when to slide over and help contest a shot.

One of the few defenders to hold his opponents to a lower field goal percentage from all areas of the court , Anunoby can truly guard every position and played a huge part in helping the Knicks win the 2026 title.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-3.8 , Steals/G: 1.4, Blocks/G: 1.5

Scottie Barnes is knocking on the door of NBA superstardom.

As good as the 25-year-old is on offense with his scoring and playmaking ability, Barnes may be even better defensively. Not only was Barnes the only player in the NBA to average at least 1.4 steals and blocks last season, he's the only one to do so in the past six seasons .

He's extremely dangerous as a help-side defender, coming over to erase shot attempts from all angles on a regular basis.

Barnes' athleticism at 6'8" and 237 pounds makes him look like a slightly shorter version of Giannis Antetokounmpo, a power forward who's able to cover a lot of ground while using his strength to handle opposing bigs one-on-one.

On a terrific Toronto Raptors team that's going to wreak havoc defensively with Kawhi Leonard and Collin Murray-Boyles, Barnes is the centerpiece and a future Defensive Player of the Year.

Defensive Swing Rating: plus-1.3 , Steals/G: 1.5, Blocks/G: 0.6

Back-to-back top-8 finishes for Defensive Players of the Year are just the start for Amen Thompson, one of the most unique defenders the NBA has ever seen.

His 6'7", 200-pound frame is one of the most athletic in the NBA, as Thompson can fly around the court like a defensive tornado, disrupting everything in his path. His 1.5 steals per game were good for 10th overall in the NBA .

Perhaps the best evidence for Thompson's defensive prowess is the fact that the Houston Rockets finished sixth overall in defensive rating last season despite having Alperen Şengün at center, 37-year-old Kevin Durant playing big minutes and injuries to Steven Adams and Fred VanVleet.

Thompson played a whopping 37.4 minutes per game (second-most in the NBA behind Tyrese Maxey) in his 79 contests, and his 2,953 total minutes were the most of any player . That's a ton of mileage for a player who was needed to defend nearly every position at times.

4. Chet Holmgren, F/C, Oklahoma City Thunder

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-8.7 , Steals/G: 0.6, Blocks/G: 1.9

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2025-26)

On a roster full of outstanding defenders, Chet Holmgren is the best of the bunch for the Oklahoma City Thunder.

He's one of the premier shot-blockers in the NBA, holding opponents to 46.4 percent shooting at the rim, the lowest mark of any of the top-56 shot contesters and even better than Victor Wembanyama. Holmgren's 1.9 blocks ranked second in the league as well.

A 7'1" frame and 7'6" wingspan can cover a lot of ground horizontally and air vertically, allowing Holmgren to contest everything inside the arc.

In a normal NBA era, we'd be talking about Holmgren as the next great defensive force. Thanks to the center in San Antonio, however, Holmgren finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and may have to stay in a very large shadow.

3. Rudy Gobert, C, Minnesota Timberwolves

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-11.8 , Steals/G: 0.8, Blocks/G: 1.6

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year x 4 (2017-18, 2018-19, 2020-21, 2023-24), All-Defensive 1st Team x 8 (2016-17, 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2023-24, 2025-26), All-Defensive 2nd Team (2024-25), Block Champion (2016-17)

Rudy Gobert will go down as one of the greatest defenders in NBA history and is tied with Ben Wallace and Dikembe Mutombo for the most Defensive Player of the Year awards ever (four).

An elite rim protector and rebounder, Gobert has anchored Utah Jazz and Minnesota Timberwolves teams for the past 13 years. He's led the NBA in blocks once and defensive rebounding twice.

Remarkably, Gobert has ranked in the 94th percentile or better in defensive swing rating in 10 of his 13 seasons, and isn't slowing down. His minus-11.8 rating ranked in the 98th percentile last year, the second-best mark of his career.

With nine total All-Defensive teams to his name, Gobert can move into a tie with Scottie Pippen for sixth place on the all-time list following another big year.

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-1.2 , Steals/G: 2.0, Blocks/G: 0.9

Honors: All-Defensive 1st Team (2025-26), Steals Champion (2025-26)

Amen Thompson may be the bigger offensive threat, although Ausar is the better defender and second-best defensive player overall in the NBA today.

No player can turn an opponent's water off like Thompson, who led the NBA in steals despite playing a modest 26.0 minutes a game. His steal rate of 3.7 percent also led the league.

In the last 17 years , only Draymond Green, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and now Thompson have averaged at least 2.0 steals and 0.9 blocks over a full season, speaking to their unique blend of defensive contributions.

1. Victor Wembanyama, C, San Antonio Spurs

Defensive Swing Rating: minus-12.3 , Steals/G: 1.0, Blocks/G: 3.1

Honors: Defensive Player of the Year (2025-26), All-Defensive 1st Team x 2 (2023-24, 2025-26), Block Champion x 3 (2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26)

Victor Wembanyama is this generation's greatest defender and could go down as the best ever by the time his career is over. If not for a deep vein thrombosis suffered during his sophomore season, the 22-year-old would be coming off back-to-back DPOYs.

A 7'4" frame, eight-foot wingspan and 9'7" standing reach means Wembanyama can contest shots without even fully raising his arms, giving the San Antonio Spurs the ultimate NBA cheat code. Wembanyama's 3.5 blocks per game for his career are tied with Mark Eaton for the highest in league history .

Teams have to completely game-plan around Wembanyama's presence, as he can switch onto guards on the wing while making other 7-footers appear small inside.

No disrespect to the rest of the field, but the entire NBA is playing for second place when it comes to Defensive Player of the Year as long as Wembanyama is in the league.

Arguably the most unique talent in the history of the league, Wembanyama is easily the NBA's best defensive player.

articles.title: The NBA's 10 Highest-Paid Players This Season
articles.summary: Some of the NBA's 10 highest-paid players for the 2026-27 season are overpaid. Some are underpaid.
articles.body:
Some of the NBA's 10 highest-paid players for the 2026-27 season are overpaid. Some are underpaid.

But the one thing they have in common, aside from at one point in the past or present being among the NBA's elite, is that they've all been in the league for at least nine seasons.

That's to be expected. Once a player has at least 10 years of NBA experience, he's eligible for a maximum contract starting at 35 percent of the salary cap.

Young stars like Victor Wembanyama and Anthony Edwards will eventually be on this list one day. But for now, the 25-and-under stars will have to wait.

When Butler signed a two-year, $111 million extension with the Golden State Warriors in February 2025, both sides had no idea he would miss a huge chunk of it with a torn ACL.

How Butler looks when he returns will be fascinating. There isn't much history of elite athletes trying to return from a torn ACL that they suffered at 36 years old.

If Butler doesn't return to his pre-injury form, the Warriors might not have enough offensive talent to win a playoff series. Butler averaged 20.0 points, 5.6 rebounds and 4.9 assists per game before suffering his injury in January.

Booker will be rising up this list in the coming years. He signed a two-year max extension that will pay him an estimated $64.7 million in 2028-29 and $67.9 million in 2029-30 (player option).

The 29-year-old has an aesthetically pleasing game due to his ability to make closely defended mid-range shots, but he's not efficient enough to warrant the kind of money he'll be making with that extension.

With that said, he offers plenty of value as a volume scorer and underrated passer. However, the Suns don't have the draft assets to surround him with the talent needed for a deep playoff run.

Karl-Anthony Towns' contract status is under the microscope right now, as he and the Knicks are reportedly far apart on what his next extension should look like.

Stefan Bondy of the New York Post reported that the Knicks offered the 30-year-old big man a four-year, $200 million extension. But he's eligible for a four-year deal worth as much as $276 million.

Towns would likely get a max or near-max deal if he declines his $61.0 million player option for the 2027-28 season and becomes an unrestricted free agent next offseason. But the grass might not be greener if Towns takes a bigger deal elsewhere in free agency.

Towns and the Knicks will likely wind up compromising for something higher than $200 million, but not close to his max.

The Celtics' decision to trade Jaylen Brown with three years left on his five-year, $285 million contract was ruthless. But was it wise?

Brown is a talented scorer, but his on/off ratings have never been impressive . The C's seemed to be conceding that his contract would age poorly, as he'll be making $65.6 million in 2028-29, which will be his age-32 campaign.

Brown can stick it to the C's by leading the 76ers on a title run this year.

Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid often appear in "worst contracts in the NBA" articles . Now, they are teammates. That is one of many reasons why the Philadelphia 76ers are the most fascinating team in the NBA this season.

Embiid is on those lists due to his injury issues. The 32-year-old has played in just 96 games over the last three seasons.

If he's healthy for the playoffs, the Sixers will have a chance to win it all. If he's injured again, he'll be back on "worst contract" lists since he's owed $62.6 million in 2027-28 and $67.3 million in 2028-29 (player option).

Jayson Tatum was not quite back to his previous form last season upon returning from his torn Achilles tendon. But all things considered, he had an impressive 16-game regular-season stint after such a serious injury.

This year, anything short of MVP-level production and impact will be disappointing.

Tatum is owed $62.8 million in 2027-28, $67.1 million in 2028-29 and $71.4 million in 2029-30 (player option). The 28-year-old is likely to be worth every penny of that contract.

It's been a wild few years for Anthony Davis.

In August 2023, Davis signed a three-year, $175.4 million extension with the Los Angeles Lakers that would keep him under contract through 2027-28.

A year-and-a-half later, the Lakers traded him to the Dallas Mavericks before that extension even began. One year after that, the Mavericks sent him to the Washington Wizards.

Davis wants one more major payday , but the Wizards probably won't give it to him as they prioritize cap space for their young core. He's expected to decline his 2027-28 player option to enter free agency and get that last bag.

Considering the 33-year-old's injury history, there might not be a long list of teams looking to pay him. But all it takes is one.

Antetokounmpo is on a guaranteed contract this season and has a $62.8 million player option in 2027-28. In theory, he could decline it and become a free agent next year.

It would be shocking if the Miami Heat's new star departs after only one season. But until he signs a long-term deal, Heat fans have every right to be nervous.

Antetokounmpo can't sign a four-year extension until Jan. 6, so nothing can be done on that front for now. The best pitch the Heat could give the 31-year-old is getting off to a dominant start.

Like Antetokounmpo, Nikola Jokić could become a free agent next offseason. He's already said that he will . But it's not because he's planning on leaving Denver.

If he extends his contract now, he'd be able to sign a four-year, $276 million deal. If he declines his player option and re-signs with the Nuggets as a free agent next offseason, he'll be eligible for a five-year deal worth more than $355 million.

The 31-year-old said at media day that he will re-sign with the Nuggets "if they want me."

Curry's reign as the NBA's highest-paid player will end after this season.

Curry was eligible for a $65.7 million salary next season, but he took a pay cut with the two-year extension he signed in September. He'll instead make $55.7 million next season.

Considering he's 38 years old and coming off a season in which he missed 39 games mostly due to runner's knee, he probably wasn't worth his max solely from an on-court perspective. That max would have paid him $71 million for the 2028-29 season.

Of course, he's been worth exponentially more than he's made over his career since he's been the biggest reason why the Warriors went from an afterthought to the NBA's most valuable franchise.

The Dubs are projected to be a cap-space team next offseason and will have better options with the $10 million pay cut Curry took. It'll be up to general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. and the Warriors' front office to take advantage of it.

articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “We never felt like we were unloved. We never felt like we didn’t have support”: How Harrison Barnes’ mother Shirley overcame homelessness to raise the NBA star
articles.summary: Success stories in the NBA often begin with talent, hard work and big moments on the court.
articles.body: Success stories in the NBA often begin with talent, hard work and big moments on the court. Harrison Barnes’ journey started with a struggle his family could not have planned for. When he was just three months old, Barnes and his mother, Shirley, became homeless after she learned she did not qualify for public housing. With little money and a baby to care for, Shirley had to find a way to give her children a stable future.Barnes eventually became an NBA champion with the Golden State Warriors, but never forgot Shirley’s sacrifices while raising him and his younger sister, Jourdan-Ashle.How Shirley Barnes faced homelessness while raising her sonShirley was 26 when she was preparing to welcome Harrison in 1991. She hoped to build a stable home, but money was tight. When Harrison was three months old, she was preparing to move into public housing. Two weeks before the planned move, officials told her she did not qualify.With few resources left, she took her baby to a homeless shelter in Ames, Iowa. “It was my first time being in a shelter,” Shirley said. She recalled having to leave at certain times of the day and share showers with other residents.“Sitting in that shelter I felt isolated, but I didn’t want pity,” she said. “My faith never wavered, I just kept praying, believing, and begging God to intercede on my behalf and help give us a chance.”The family eventually moved into Section 8 housing in Ames, and Shirley found work at Iowa State University. Money remained tight. They searched between car seats for petrol money, and basketball registration fees added pressure. Harrison was too young to remember the shelter, but he grew up knowing how hard his mother worked to give him and his sister a loving home. How Shirley helped Harrison Barnes’ pursue his basketball dreamShirley did not play basketball, but she and Jourdan-Ashle spent hours rebounding for Harrison. She bought instructional videos to help him improve and began filming his games around seventh grade. The family watched the footage together, even though Shirley was often tired from work.“Growing up in a single home, income is low,” Barnes said. “She was working, she was tired, but she put all of that on the side to always be there to support me, whether I was in seventh grade, high school, at North Carolina or in the NBA.”Basketball was not cheap. Shirley wanted Harrison to follow his passion, but she also had bills to pay. When he was in fifth grade, he got a job working for a local farmer and began saving. At one point, he had $1,000.Shirley first told him to keep the money, but household bills eventually led her to ask him to contribute. “Money was so tight that we were looking for pennies between the seats in the car just to make ends meet,” she said.Barnes became a top high school prospect, played for the University of North Carolina and was selected seventh by the Golden State Warriors in the 2012 NBA Draft. He won a championship with the team in 2015. Why Harrison Barnes says his mother shaped his valuesBarnes never forgot his mother’s sacrifices or the way she helped others. Shirley started Suited For Work Clothing Closet, providing free clothing and accessories to unemployed people preparing for job interviews. Harrison and Jourdan-Ashle helped organise donations, and the experience stayed with him.“It really made an impression on me,” Barnes said. “That’s why now I do a lot of non-profit and charitable work because I saw the sacrifice and giving mentality that she had an early age.”In Sept. 2018, the Mavericks and Barnes contributed $100,000 to Helping Hands for Single Moms Dallas. The donation was announced at a “My Mom, My Hero” event honouring Shirley and other mothers raising children while working to build stable homes. The programme aimed to help single mothers in North Texas with expenses and barriers that could affect their education and daily lives.For Barnes, the event was a chance to recognise the person who had supported him long before he became an NBA player. How Shirley Barnes' story became a message of hopeAt the 2018 event, Shirley offered a message to other single mothers facing difficult circumstances. “Times are tough, but this will pass,” she said. “Never waiver. You will make it.”She encouraged mothers to build a network of people who could help them through hard periods. “Surround yourself with a circle of support and a network. A village,” she said.Barnes said marriage helped him understand what his mother had taken on as a single parent. “My mom didn’t complain, even when she was tired. I am sure there were days she wished she could have raised my sister and I with somebody. But she gave us one of the very best home… probably the best home that we could ever imagine,” he said.He remembered how she made sure her children never felt short of love or support. “We never felt like we were unloved,” Barnes said. “We never felt like we didn’t have support.”That was the foundation Shirley wanted to give her children, regardless of the family’s finances. At the Mavericks event, she received an award recognising her commitment to her family.How Harrison Barnes carried his mother’s example into his careerBarnes’ NBA journey brought him a championship, but he sees his mother’s support as part of that success. Shirley made sacrifices to keep him playing and taught him to care about people beyond his own family.The experience of homelessness did not disappear from their past. It became part of a wider story about persistence, support and helping others. Shirley kept working when she was tired, made sure her children felt loved and continued giving back to her community.The little boy she once carried into a homeless shelter grew up to become an NBA player who could use his platform to support other families. Honouring his mother was not only about recognising her sacrifices. It was also about carrying her values forward.Barnes’ championship will remain part of his career, but Shirley’s influence began long before the NBA.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
